terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, transitive: aliquem ad aliquid, in aliquid, or ut + subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Brut. 19: impulsī atque incēnsī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally to push or strike; of the mind, the usual word in good prose for what moves someone to act (Lewis & Short). The reason is the subject: quae rēs tē ad hoc impulit?, what made you do this?
Literally to set in rapid motion (horses, ships); of people and their zeal, to stir up and spur on.

phrases.latin: ad quam quemque artem putābat esse aptum, ad eam impellere atque hortārī solēbat
phrases.english: whatever art he thought each of us was fitted for, he would drive and encourage us towards it

phrases.latin: quōrum studiō legendī meum scrībendī studium in diēs incitātur
phrases.english: whose eagerness to read spurs on my eagerness to write from day to day

sources: Lewis & Short: impello · Lewis & Short: incito · Lewis & Short: concito
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 348.
